target.name: Joscha Bach, Hikari Sorensen
target.title: The Machine Consciousness Hypothesis
target.date_type: Selected PDF version date, not initial article date
target.quote: Consciousness sorts things and animals into different kinds, identifies and tracks individuals, and gives each their names.

L1.analysis: Partial conceptual and operational correspondence: spatial features become individuated/categorized objects within a model. Tracking and motion prediction are related temporal operations, not identical algorithms.

L2.analysis: Common ordered subchain: organize spatial distinctions -> construct object representations -> maintain or predict an object over change. SAN links it to paired brain/computer measurement; MCH embeds it in a genesis story.

L3.constrained_conclusion: The target output is categorized objects whose individual identity can be tracked over change, not just a list of object names.
L3.required_operations: There must be an operation relating perceptual distinctions to an object representation, and some way to preserve or update object identity across changing observations.
L3.alternative_routes: A feed-forward classifier with a separate tracker, a recurrent scene model, and predictive object tracking can satisfy parts of that requirement without the same genesis or consciousness mechanism.
L3.source_test: SAN lines 71–79 explicitly group lines into a car and predict its motion; lines 169–189 describe a spatial representation changing over time. This supplies the object-building and temporal-relation subset.
L3.remaining_indeterminacy: The backward test supports a partial object-processing relation. It does not force MCH to use SAN’s BCI measurement procedure or prove identical tracking and prediction algorithms.
L3.analysis: Work backward from recognizing the same moving individual: the system must retain discriminative features and link observations across change; grouped object representations are a compatible route. Output does not determine a unique representation, consciousness mechanism, thalamic code, or influence.
L3.constrained_target_output: Named/categorized individuals remain identifiable as their positions or appearances change.

rows.formal: Qualitative partial trace: features -> object-in-space -> temporal object relation. No equality of update functions, full simulation, functor or bisimulation is proved.
rows.residual: The SAN passage does not here present MCH's second-order-perception genesis mechanism. MCH does not here give SAN's joint external-scene/neural-measurement BCI procedure. Shared categorization alone is historically broad.

L3.constrained_conclusion: The target constructs a perceptual world from simultaneously maintained partial models, despite their incompleteness and potential conflict.
L3.required_operations: Contributions from more than one partial representation must affect an organized output; the target additionally requires a way to reduce inconsistency between those contributions.
L3.alternative_routes: Completion from stored expectations, a feed-forward integrator, and iterative constraint repair are possible routes. A shared completed-world output alone cannot select which repair rule is used.

L3.analysis: Work backward from a stable scene built from partial, potentially incompatible models: contributions must be represented and their conflicts must be handled by reconciliation, weighting, exclusion or suppression. The monologue's internally supplied context and converging senses support the integration portion, but do not specify that conflict-handling operation. Sensory completion and alternative model-selection schemes could yield the bounded perceptual output; neither the output nor the source fixes CIMC's attention/repair implementation.

rows.formal: Partial input/transform/output alignment of sensory-and-internal contributions -> integration -> scene; no proof that the two integration operators implement the same optimization.

target.name: Joscha Bach, Hikari Sorensen
target.title: The Machine Consciousness Hypothesis
target.date_type: Selected PDF version date, not initial article date
target.quote: By characterizing consciousness as an operator on mental states, we can approach its functionality by observing how mental states change as a result of conscious operation.

L1.analysis: Partial process correspondence at the state-transition level. SAN specifies a current/desired comparison and proposed external write-in; MCH characterizes internally conscious operation by its effects on mental state.

L2.analysis: Shared narrow subchain: a represented mental state -> an operation on that state -> changed mental content. The controller and cause of the operation differ, so this is not a match of the whole control architecture.

L3.constrained_conclusion: The target treats conscious operation as capable of changing a mental state.
L3.required_operations: At minimum, there must be distinguishable before/after mental states and an effective transformation between them. This alone does not require an explicitly represented goal or a difference message.
L3.alternative_routes: Externally induced change, autonomous control, and spontaneous internal state evolution can instantiate state transitions; only further constraints distinguish those causes.
L3.source_test: SAN lines 497–507 provide a concrete proposed transformation: compare the current pattern with an intended one, then transmit a change that alters experienced content.
L3.remaining_indeterminacy: This is a broad partial state-transition framing, not identity between an external BCI operator and conscious agency. No target-specific controller can be reconstructed from this shared endpoint alone.
L3.analysis: Given a changed mental state, some effective transition must have occurred; that observation alone neither entails a desired-state comparator nor a difference-coded signal. MCH's more constrained coherent output is compatible with many repair operations. A full delta-controller cannot be reverse-inferred.
L3.constrained_target_output: Conscious operation changes mental states; the surrounding target account associates the change with increased coherence.

rows.formal: Abstract partial transition correspondence s -> operation -> s′. The SAN transition carries a specified desired state and difference message; those labels have no exact mapped MCH operator here.
rows.residual: MCH does not specify a current/desired difference or an external BCI channel in this passage. SAN's difference-write proposal is not a demonstration of consciousness's own control process.

target.quote: the capacity of a system to exert control over future states, that is, to select among possible actions on the basis of internal representations of goals, preferences, or evaluative criteria.

L1.analysis: Partial operational correspondence: represent a goal or desired pattern -> choose the change relative to it -> influence a subsequent state. SAN supplies a particular difference-write procedure; CIMC supplies an abstract agency definition.

L2.analysis: Shared control subchain: represented future condition -> selection of action/update -> changed state. It bridges BCI and agency contexts without claiming that the external BCI controller is the target's self-organizing agent.

L3.constrained_conclusion: The target selects actions on the basis of represented goals in order to control future states.
L3.required_operations: A represented preference or intended condition must influence which action is selected, and that action must be capable of changing a subsequent state.
L3.alternative_routes: A learned policy, model-predictive control, and a direct state-difference update can meet that goal-sensitive control requirement. The abstract definition does not require subtraction of neural patterns.
L3.source_test: SAN lines 501–507 represent the desired perceptual pattern, compare it with the ongoing pattern and choose the transmitted update accordingly. The source therefore meets the goal-conditioned update subset.
L3.remaining_indeterminacy: BCI versus autonomous agency is an implementation/context residual, not a veto on the shared control subchain. Matching objectives, policies and the complete agent remain unproved.
L3.analysis: Work backward from selective control toward a represented goal: the selected intervention must be sensitive to an evaluative criterion and capable of affecting the outcome. This permits delta control, planning, policy selection or other strategies; it does not require the source's difference-signal protocol.
L3.constrained_target_output: A system selects among possible actions using represented goals/preferences and thereby controls future states.

rows.formal: Partial control schema: (current state, represented goal) -> selected action/update -> subsequent state. Identical objectives, transition kernels and goal evaluation are not proved.
rows.residual: CIMC's definition does not mandate a neural pattern difference, receiver-specific write-in or external interface. The correspondence is one subchain of goal-directed control, not proof of the complete SAN architecture.

target.name: Joscha Bach, Hikari Sorensen
target.title: The Machine Consciousness Hypothesis
target.date_type: Selected PDF version date, not initial article date
target.quote: The contents of consciousness may be experienced as real or imaginary

L1.analysis: Partial conceptual/output correspondence: an internal representational state can contain an object without that object being present in the external environment. The target separately describes a variable realness dimension.

L2.analysis: SAN: state-dependent neural intervention -> added experienced object. MCH: representational content -> real/imaginary character. The shared endpoint is represented experience rather than necessary external presence; the causal routes are not fully aligned.

L3.constrained_conclusion: The target distinguishes experienced content from its real or imaginary character.
L3.required_operations: Content must be represented in a way that does not simply equate its occurrence in experience with the external presence of the represented object.
L3.alternative_routes: Imagining an object, an induced percept and assigning a realness property can all dissociate content from external presence, but they need not use the same process.
L3.source_test: SAN lines 505–519 propose changing neural content so an object not externally present enters experienced reality. That is an explicit instance of the representational distinction.
L3.remaining_indeterminacy: The backward inference preserves the partial output/conceptual match. It does not establish that induced experience, imagination and MCH’s realness dimension are identical.
L3.analysis: Work backward from experiencing an externally absent object: an internal content-carrying process must support that appearance independently of that object's present sensory cause. Dreams, hallucinations, imagery or intervention could do so; no specific pattern-difference input or realness variable is forced.
L3.constrained_target_output: Conscious content can be imagined or experienced as factual even when an external object does not warrant that appearance.

rows.formal: Partial output relation between internally represented object and external-object presence; no equivalence of hallucination, imagination or realness-detection operators.
rows.residual: The target's claim concerns the representational character of experience, not this specific neural intervention. An induced percept, imagined content and an experience of factuality must not be conflated.

L3.analysis: Work backward from mutually confirmed coordination: receiving units must affect the subsequent exchange, and a returned signal must bear on whether a proposed communication or state is accepted. The monologue supplies a compatible return-check motif. Its delivery acknowledgement alone cannot establish consistency of represented contents; acknowledgements, negotiation, consensus and other feedback protocols can differ in what they certify.
